title: Bohr Model of the Atom

references.label: NCERT Physics Part II, Class 12 — Atoms

summary: Bohr's model explains the hydrogen atom's discrete line spectrum by postulating that electrons orbit the nucleus only in specific, quantized energy levels, jumping between them by absorbing or emitting a photon of exactly the right energy.
explanation: Bohr's model (an early quantum model, later refined/replaced by full quantum mechanics but still useful for hydrogen-like systems) postulates that an electron can orbit the nucleus only in certain ALLOWED, quantized orbits, where its angular momentum is an integer multiple of h/2π (mvr = nh/2π, n = 1, 2, 3...) — this quantization condition is what restricts electrons to only specific energy levels rather than any arbitrary orbit. While in one of these allowed (stationary) orbits, the electron does NOT radiate energy despite being in constant circular motion (a direct contradiction of classical electromagnetic theory, which predicts an accelerating charge should continuously radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus) — Bohr simply POSTULATED this stability as a new rule, without deriving it from more fundamental principles (that had to wait for full quantum mechanics). Energy of the nth orbit in a hydrogen-like atom is En = −13.6Z²/n² eV (Z = atomic number, n = principal quantum number) — NEGATIVE, since the electron is bound to the nucleus, with energy becoming less negative (approaching zero) as n increases, meaning the electron becomes progressively less tightly bound in higher orbits. An electron can JUMP between allowed orbits by absorbing (jumping to a higher n) or emitting (falling to a lower n) a photon whose energy exactly equals the difference between the two orbit energies, ΔE = Ef − Ei = hν — this explains why atomic emission/absorption spectra show discrete, sharp LINES (only specific photon energies/frequencies are allowed) rather than a continuous spectrum, directly matching the experimentally observed hydrogen spectral series (Lyman, Balmer, Paschen, etc., corresponding to transitions ending at different final n values). Bohr's model works well ONLY for hydrogen and other hydrogen-LIKE (single-electron) species (like He⁺, Li²⁺); it fails to correctly predict spectra for multi-electron atoms, where electron-electron repulsion effects require full quantum mechanical treatment.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming Bohr's model applies accurately to ALL atoms — it works well only for hydrogen and hydrogen-like (single electron) species; multi-electron atoms need full quantum mechanics due to electron-electron interactions the simple model ignores.

Believing an electron radiates energy continuously while in a stable (stationary) Bohr orbit — Bohr's model specifically POSTULATES that electrons in these allowed orbits do NOT radiate energy, resolving the classical instability problem by simple assumption rather than derivation.

Forgetting that atomic spectral lines correspond to SPECIFIC energy differences between allowed levels, not a continuous range — this is exactly why atomic emission/absorption spectra appear as discrete lines rather than a continuous spectrum.
examples: An electron falling from n=3 to n=2 in a hydrogen atom emits a specific-wavelength photon that appears as one of the visible lines in the hydrogen Balmer series.
The energy required to completely remove an electron from the ground state (n=1) of hydrogen — the ionization energy — is exactly 13.6 eV, matching En = −13.6/n² at n=1.
genZNote: Bohr's electrons: quantum-locked into specific orbits, no in-between allowed.
